::: {.status}
**Version 0.1.** Near consensus at ACLCA 2026: if AI contributed to a study, say so. The point is reproducibility, not confession.
:::

## AI-compiled versus AI-generated

An **AI-compiled** value was found and assembled by AI from sources you can check. An **AI-generated** value has no source outside the model. Compiled values are disclosed and cited. Generated values should generally not be in your inventory at all.

## What to declare

Copy this into the methods section or an appendix of your report or paper, and fill in each item.

```
AI use disclosure (working group template v0.1)

1. Where AI was used: tasks (literature search, data extraction,
   dataset mapping, gap filling, code, drafting) and which results
   or numbers each task affected.
2. Which system: tool or model name, version, and date of use;
   whether a confidential, non-training endpoint was used for
   proprietary data.
3. Compiled or generated: for each AI-assisted value, whether it
   was compiled from citable sources (cite them) or model-estimated
   (give the method and its range of validity).
4. Verification: who reviewed what, against which sources or
   calculations, and what was corrected.
5. Repeatability: whether rerunning the AI step gives the same
   answer, and if not, how the reported value was fixed.
6. Uncertainty: how model-estimated values were treated, and
   whether they were included in sensitivity analysis.
7. Responsibility: the named practitioner who signs for the
   numbers. AI assistance does not transfer responsibility.
```

## A note on the minority view

Some practitioners argue disclosure is unnecessary because the signing human is always responsible, as with any search tool. The professional engineers at the session drew the opposite conclusion: because they stamp and seal results, they must be able to show how every number was obtained. Disclosure is part of that due diligence. Regulation is also moving this way; one respondent noted the EU AI Act already requires disclosure in some contexts.
